paragraphs: Angular Steering addresses how to change a language model’s behavior while preserving its broader language abilities. Existing approaches modify internal activations by adding a feature direction or removing a component along it. The paper argues that these operations can be sensitive to parameter choices and can unintentionally interact with unrelated features.

The proposed method expresses steering as a rotation within a fixed two-dimensional activation subspace. Rotating toward or away from a behavior direction provides a continuous way to adjust its influence. The authors demonstrate refusal and emotion steering. An adaptive version applies rotations selectively to activations already aligned with the target feature, aiming to improve stability and coherence.

The paper places addition and orthogonalization methods within a shared geometric framework, making steering parameters easier to manage. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes report robust behavioral control while retaining general language modeling performance. These findings support rotation as a flexible control mechanism over the tested adjustments, rather than establishing that every behavioral intervention preserves all capabilities.
neurips-2025-angular-steering-behavior-c.tldr: Angular Steering controls language-model behavior through activation rotations, with experiments showing stable adjustments while preserving general language modeling performance.

paragraphs: Brain Harmony, also called BrainHarmonix, combines information about brain structure and activity in a shared representation. Structural MRI describes morphology, while functional MRI records changing activity. The model follows two motivating principles: these modalities supply complementary information, and brain structure shapes functional dynamics. Its goal is to capture both within compact, continuous one-dimensional tokens.

Pretraining first develops each modality separately with geometric pre-alignment, then connects them through shared brain hub tokens. A dynamics encoder accommodates functional scans collected with different repetition times, allowing it to handle variation in their temporal sampling. The training data include 64,594 structural MRI volumes and 70,933 functional MRI time series.

The resulting latent representation compresses high-dimensional neuroimaging signals into a common space for downstream tasks. The authors report strong generalization and consistent improvements over previous approaches in disorder classification and cognition prediction. These findings support combining morphology and function for reusable brain representations, with the reported benefits spanning both neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative classification tasks.
neurips-2025-brain-harmony-a-multimodal-.tldr: BrainHarmonix compresses structural and functional brain scans into shared tokens, improving reported results on disorder classification and cognition prediction.

paragraphs: ComPO studies how to align language models using preference pairs when those pairs contain noise. The paper connects this problem to verbosity and likelihood displacement in direct alignment methods. In particular, preferred and dispreferred responses can receive similar likelihoods, making the distinction supplied by a preference label difficult to use effectively.

The proposed alternative uses comparison oracles within zeroth-order optimization: optimization proceeds through comparisons rather than directly relying on gradient information from the objective. The authors provide convergence guarantees for a basic version of the method. They then introduce heuristics to make a practical version more flexible and compatible with language-model alignment.

Experiments cover both base and instruction-tuned versions of Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Gemma-2-9B, evaluated on AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Arena-Hard. The reported results support ComPO as an alternative for learning from noisy preferences. A central finding is that preference pairs with different likelihood margins benefit from specialized treatment. The theoretical guarantee concerns the basic scheme, while the enhanced practical scheme is supported by experiments.
neurips-2025-compo-preference-alignment-.tldr: ComPO uses comparison-based optimization for preference alignment, with theoretical guarantees for its basic scheme and empirical support under noisy preferences.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion combines diffusion models with tree search to explore possible trajectories. Its planning range is constrained by the trajectory lengths used during training. Replanning can join shorter plans into a longer sequence, but the underlying search still operates inside individual trajectories and lacks a view of the overall composition.

C-MCTD changes the unit of planning from one trajectory to a composition of trajectories. Its Online Composer searches over complete plan compositions, giving the planning process access to global context. This addresses the distinction between simply concatenating locally chosen segments and reasoning about those segments together as parts of one plan.

Two additional components address the cost of that broader search. The Distributed Composer explores from multiple starting points in parallel to reduce search complexity. The Preplan Composer reuses cached plan graphs to accelerate inference. Together, the components target global coordination, search cost, and reuse of prior planning work. The abstract presents this framework and its intended computational benefits without reporting numerical planning results.
neurips-2025-compositional-monte-carlo-t.tldr: C-MCTD extends diffusion-based planning by searching over complete plan compositions, using parallel exploration and cached plan graphs to manage computation.

paragraphs: Safe linear bandits describe repeated decisions in which both the reward objective and the constraints are unknown. An agent must learn which actions perform well while managing constraint violations. Existing approaches offer strong regret guarantees, but their action-selection steps can require expensive optimization, making computational cost a central obstacle.

COLTS selects actions by solving linear programs with added perturbations. The framework has two variants with different information requirements. Given a safe action, S-COLTS guarantees zero risk and regret bounded by approximately the square root of d cubed times T, apart from logarithmic factors. R-COLTS needs no instance information and obtains that same order for both regret and risk, where d is dimension and T is the number of rounds.

The analysis uses coupled noise to produce frequent local optimism about the optimum, together with a scaling argument for changing constraints across rounds. Simulations report performance matching or exceeding existing safe-bandit methods with substantially better scalability. The result offers less expensive action selection while preserving the stated guarantees, with the zero-risk guarantee specifically depending on access to a safe action.
neurips-2025-constrained-linear-thompson.tldr: COLTS uses perturbed linear programs for efficient safe-bandit decisions, offering distinct guarantees with and without a known safe action.

paragraphs: COUPLE addresses alignment with multiple human values whose priorities vary across people and communities. The paper argues that treating values as independent and equally important misses both their relationships and their relative importance. It also identifies a steering problem: models can struggle to express precise value priorities, especially priorities that are underrepresented.

The framework introduces a structural causal model that explicitly represents dependencies, priorities, and connections between high-level value dimensions and behavior. Counterfactual reasoning then guides generation toward a specified value objective. This gives the method a structured way to reason about how a different desired value configuration should affect the output.

Explicit causal modeling also provides an interpretable account of the relationships used for steering. Evaluation on two datasets with different value systems reports improvements over baselines across diverse objective types. The findings support modeling value interactions when seeking fine-grained control. Although the framework is designed to accommodate arbitrary desired value objectives, the reported empirical evidence comes from the evaluated datasets and objectives.
neurips-2025-counterfactual-reasoning-fo.tldr: COUPLE combines causal modeling and counterfactual reasoning to steer language models toward differing, interdependent value priorities.

paragraphs: Curly Flow Matching studies how to infer a system’s movement from observations of populations at different times. The paper challenges the usual least-action assumption, which leads to gradient-field dynamics and energy-minimizing trajectories. Such dynamics cannot represent the periodic, non-gradient behavior found in some natural systems, including cell cycles.

Curly-FM changes the reference process used in a Schrödinger bridge formulation. Instead of starting with a zero-drift process, it constructs one with nonzero drift using inferred velocities alongside population snapshots. Those velocity estimates supply information about motion that population distributions alone do not express, allowing the learned dynamics to include circulation and other non-gradient behavior.

The authors demonstrate trajectory inference for single cells, computational fluid dynamics, and ocean currents using approximate velocities. They report trajectories that better agree with both the reference process and the observed population marginals. The contribution is therefore about capturing how populations move as well as matching where they are observed, with inferred velocity information playing a central role in the approach.
neurips-2025-curly-flow-matching-for-lea.tldr: Curly-FM uses inferred velocities and a nonzero-drift reference process to learn dynamics that can include periodic, non-gradient motion.

paragraphs: Multicalibration asks a predictor to remain calibrated across many overlapping subpopulations. Common methods divide prediction values into discrete bins and repeatedly adjust outputs. The paper identifies several costs of this strategy: rounding error, a sensitive choice of bin size, and possible distortions that can affect later decisions based on the predictions.

The proposed method directly minimizes an empirical risk objective over ensembles of depth-two decision trees. It therefore fits within a conventional training workflow and can use existing tree-ensemble software such as LightGBM. Avoiding output discretization removes the need to choose a binning granularity as part of this calibration procedure.

The theoretical multicalibration guarantee requires a distributional condition called loss saturation. The authors report that the condition held throughout their evaluations across multiple datasets; this observation does not make it an unconditional assumption. Empirically, the method matches or improves on existing approaches, including under a discretized evaluation metric whose granularity matches the baselines. The results support direct loss minimization as a practical route to multicalibration.
neurips-2025-discretization-free-multica.tldr: The paper achieves multicalibration through tree-ensemble loss minimization without output binning, with a guarantee conditional on loss saturation.

paragraphs: Dyn-O builds world models that represent an environment through its objects. The motivation is that many changes in an environment arise from interactions among objects, so a structured representation may help model those changes. Earlier object-centric world models were largely explored in visually simple settings, leaving their effectiveness in richer scenes less established.

The proposed system improves both the learning of object-centric representations and the prediction of their dynamics. It learns directly from pixel observations in the Procgen games, providing a test in more challenging visual environments. The paper reports higher rollout prediction accuracy than DreamerV3, meaning its predicted sequences more accurately capture subsequent observations in that evaluation.

Dyn-O also separates object features into components that are dynamic-agnostic and dynamic-aware. This separation supports more precise manipulation of the representation and enables more varied imagined trajectories. The stated findings demonstrate stronger prediction and controllable imagination in the tested environments. Compositional generalization motivates the object-centric approach, while rollout accuracy and trajectory diversity are the specific outcomes highlighted in the abstract.
neurips-2025-dyn-o-building-structured-w.tldr: Dyn-O learns object-centric world models from pixels, improving Procgen rollout prediction and enabling finer control over imagined trajectories.

paragraphs: Small Object Image Retrieval asks a search system to find images containing a particular small object within a cluttered scene. The difficulty is representing all relevant objects using a single descriptor for each image. That compact representation supports efficient search, but it must still preserve information about objects occupying only a small part of the scene.

The paper first examines weaknesses in existing retrieval methods and introduces benchmarks for this task. Its proposed framework uses a dedicated multi-object pretraining stage, followed by refinement with attention-based feature extraction and object masks. Information from multiple objects is integrated into one unified descriptor, keeping the representation suited to scalable image retrieval.

The authors report substantial improvements over existing retrieval methods and strong baselines in both zero-shot evaluation and lightweight multi-object fine-tuning. These results suggest that explicitly preparing a representation to capture multiple objects helps small objects remain useful for retrieval. The work contributes both an evaluation setting for this search problem and a training-and-refinement approach designed around its central representation challenge.
neurips-2025-find-your-needle-small-obje.tldr: Multi-object pretraining and mask-guided attention improve retrieval of images containing small objects while retaining one descriptor per image.

paragraphs: A retrieval-augmented question-answering system depends on several linked decisions: how to rewrite a query, which documents to retrieve, what information to keep, and how to produce an answer. Training these components separately can leave them pursuing objectives that do not align with the quality of the final response. A locally successful decision may therefore fail to help the complete pipeline.

MMOA-RAG treats the components as cooperating reinforcement-learning agents. They optimize a shared reward tied to the final answer, such as its F1 score. This makes overall answer quality the common objective and explicitly addresses interactions among modules, extending beyond approaches focused on individual components or simpler two-component pipelines.

Experiments on multiple question-answering benchmarks report improved pipeline performance over existing baselines. Ablation studies support the contributions of individual components and show adaptation to different pipelines and benchmarks. The findings indicate that coordinating module training can improve the assembled system, with the evidence coming from the tested configurations rather than a guarantee for every possible RAG design.
neurips-2025-improving-retrieval-augment.tldr: MMOA-RAG jointly trains RAG components as cooperating agents rewarded for final-answer quality, improving results across tested question-answering benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper learns time-series representations without relying on strong handcrafted data augmentations. Such augmentations usually provide different views of a sample, but choosing them requires knowledge of which signal changes should preserve meaning. Those choices also impose invariances on the learned representation, potentially restricting how well it generalizes.

The proposed method creates views by expressing samples through orthonormal bases and overcomplete frames. These alternative representation spaces introduce different geometric biases. The authors show that the resulting embeddings occupy distinct manifolds, and their method jointly uses the complementary geometry of those manifolds. View diversity therefore comes from how samples are represented, rather than from strong artificial changes to the data.

Evaluation covers nine datasets across five temporal sequence tasks, where signal-specific properties make augmentation design particularly difficult. The paper reports gains of up to 15–20% over existing self-supervised approaches. Those are the largest reported gains, not a uniform improvement across every task. The findings support representation geometry as a useful source of complementary learning signals without augmentation-induced diversity.
neurips-2025-learning-without-augmenting.tldr: The method learns time-series representations from complementary frame projections, reporting gains without strong handcrafted augmentations.

paragraphs: This paper addresses memory allocation inside Fourier-transform implementations used in deep learning. A real FFT takes n real inputs and produces n/2 + 1 complex outputs, creating a mismatch between input and output layouts. The authors identify this mismatch as an obstacle to fully in-place computation, which would reuse the original storage.

Their real-domain FFT framework, rdFFT, preserves an n-to-n layout. It uses symmetry in butterfly operations and conjugate relationships in the frequency domain to encode complex information implicitly. This design eliminates intermediate cache usage. The paper theoretically derives a 50% memory reduction relative to real FFTs for the proposed method.

The framework also supports parameter updates without intermediate caches by using a Fourier-transform derivative property to compute matrix inverses efficiently. Experiments on several natural language understanding tasks report lower memory overhead while maintaining model performance. The stated theoretical saving concerns the FFT method, while the application results support its usefulness for lightweight adaptation in the frequency domain; they do not claim that every training system’s total memory is halved.
neurips-2025-memory-efficient-training-w.tldr: rdFFT preserves input-output size for fully in-place Fourier computation, theoretically reducing FFT memory use by 50% relative to rFFT.

paragraphs: MesaTask addresses the creation of tabletop scenes suited to particular robot manipulation instructions. A useful training scene must contain appropriate objects and arrange them in ways that fit the task. Manual layout construction is slow, while purely random placement can produce scenes that are implausible or poorly connected to the requested activity.

The paper introduces MesaTask-10K, a dataset of approximately 10,700 synthetic scenes with manually crafted layouts and detailed relations among objects. It also proposes a Spatial Reasoning Chain that breaks scene generation into three stages: inferring the required objects, reasoning about their spatial relationships, and constructing a scene graph for the final three-dimensional layout.

MesaTask uses a language model to follow this chain and incorporates direct preference optimization to improve generation. Experiments report better task conformity and layout realism than the evaluated baselines. The contribution connects high-level instructions to explicit spatial structure, making object relationships part of the generation process. The dataset supplies examples of those relationships, while the framework uses structured reasoning to produce task-relevant scenes.
neurips-2025-mesatask-towards-task-drive.tldr: MesaTask combines a curated tabletop dataset with staged spatial reasoning to generate realistic scenes aligned with robot-task descriptions.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions to partial differential equations by checking how well their predictions satisfy the equations at sampled points. Adaptive sampling often emphasizes points with large residuals, where the equation is poorly satisfied. Although this can improve efficiency and accuracy, it can also neglect points with medium or small residuals.

The paper investigates the stability consequences of that imbalance as model complexity increases. Its analysis shows that high-residual sampling approaches need tighter bounds on the learning rate to remain stable. The proposed Langevin dynamics-based Adaptive Sampling framework, LAS, addresses this problem and is designed to tolerate a wider range of learning rates and model complexities.

Experiments report better relative L2 error and stability than existing approaches across the evaluated environments. These include high-dimensional equations, where Monte Carlo integration-based methods can become unstable. The findings make sampling strategy part of the stability discussion: choosing where to enforce the equation affects both solution error and how reliably training proceeds. The reported robustness spans the tested settings, rather than all learning rates or equation types.
neurips-2025-mitigating-instability-in-h.tldr: LAS uses Langevin dynamics for adaptive PINN sampling, improving reported accuracy and stability over methods that concentrate on high residuals.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization occurs when a student trained on a weaker teacher’s imperfect labels nevertheless outperforms that teacher. This paper studies simple mathematical models to identify mechanisms that can make this possible. Its results explain several routes to improvement rather than claiming that learning from a weaker teacher always succeeds.

The first mechanism concerns regularization. In ridge linear regression, the authors prove that a student can compensate for a teacher that regularizes too little and attain lower test error. They also show that the models’ parameterization regimes can produce qualitatively different behavior. A weighted ridge analysis identifies another route: the student’s regularization structure can align better with the target function than the teacher’s does.

The third mechanism appears in a nonlinear multi-index learning setting. A student can obtain easier task-specific features from the teacher while using broader pretraining to learn difficult features the teacher cannot capture. Together, the analyses show how teacher supervision and student capabilities can play different roles. Improvement can arise from the student’s learning constraints or prior knowledge, even though its labels originate from a weaker model.
neurips-2025-on-the-mechanisms-of-weak-t.tldr: The paper identifies regularization and pretrained feature learning as mechanisms that can let students outperform weaker teachers in analyzed models.

paragraphs: This paper asks how narrow a deep neural network can be while still approximating continuously differentiable functions. The approximation criterion controls both function values and first derivatives through the W^{1, infinity} Sobolev norm. Matching derivatives makes the question stronger than ordinary approximation of continuous functions, where only output values need to be close.

The proof strategy has two stages. First, tools from control theory establish that deep, narrow multilayer perceptrons can approximate diffeomorphisms, which are smooth invertible transformations with smooth inverses. Second, the authors combine the Borsuk-Ulam theorem with differential geometry to determine optimal widths for approximating arbitrary continuously differentiable functions through such transformations.

In certain cases, the resulting width is min(n + m, max(2n + 1, m)), where n and m are the input and output dimensions. The abstract explicitly includes dimensions (8, 8) and (16, 8), and states that the results cover a broad class of activation functions. The contribution establishes sharp width requirements in the covered cases, without asserting that this formula resolves every dimensional setting.
neurips-2025-optimal-minimum-width-for-t.tldr: The paper establishes optimal widths in certain cases for deep networks approximating both continuously differentiable functions and their first derivatives.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning in two-player zero-sum games using Optimistic Fictitious Play. Its central question is whether optimism can deliver very fast regret guarantees without regularization. Earlier constant-regret results for Optimistic Follow-the-Regularized-Leader relied on a regularized algorithm and a bounded stepsize parameter.

For two-strategy games, the authors prove that Optimistic Fictitious Play has constant regret under any tiebreaking rule. Constant regret means the accumulated shortfall measured by regret remains bounded as play continues. The proof examines payoff vectors geometrically in a dual space and identifies an energy function that stays bounded over the sequence of updates.

The paper also establishes a lower bound of order square root of T for Alternating Fictitious Play. Within the unregularized setting, this separates optimism from alternation: the former achieves the stated constant bound for two-strategy games, while the latter faces the lower bound. The result shows that an algorithm lacking a general no-regret property can still learn rapidly in this structured game setting.
neurips-2025-optimism-without-regulariza.tldr: Optimistic Fictitious Play achieves constant regret in two-strategy zero-sum games without regularization, regardless of its tiebreaking rule.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates a small synthetic training set intended to retain the usefulness of a much larger dataset. The paper argues that matching only broad statistics, such as means and variances, can miss differences between individual examples and variation within a class. Those details matter because they help define the structure a model must learn.

The method frames distillation as minimizing an optimal transport distance, aligning distributions at both global and individual-example levels. It applies this idea throughout the pipeline: transport-guided diffusion sampling aligns image latent distributions, soft relabeling adapts label distributions to the complexity of generated images, and transport-based logit matching aligns student outputs with those soft labels.

Experiments across multiple architectures and large datasets report consistent improvements over leading approaches with efficient operation. On ImageNet-1K with ten images per class, the abstract reports at least a 4% accuracy improvement for each tested architecture. The findings support preserving distributional geometry across image generation, labeling, and model training, so the compact dataset carries more than aggregate class statistics.
neurips-2025-optimizing-distributional-g.tldr: The method uses optimal transport throughout dataset distillation to preserve fine-grained variation and improve training from compact synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: PAFlow generates three-dimensional molecules conditioned on a target protein. The paper identifies two problems in existing generative approaches: unstable probability dynamics and generated molecules whose size does not fit the target pocket’s geometry. These can undermine consistent molecular quality and target compatibility, motivating a generation process that uses more explicit protein information.

The model uses flow matching and introduces a conditional formulation for discrete atom types. A protein–ligand interaction predictor guides the generation vector field toward regions associated with stronger affinity. Separately, an atom-number predictor uses information about the protein pocket to choose a molecule size better suited to that geometry.

On CrossDocked2020, the authors report state-of-the-art binding-affinity results, with an average Vina score reaching −8.31, while maintaining favorable molecular properties. This supports the combination of interaction guidance and learned molecule size in the benchmark setting. The reported affinity result is expressed through Vina scoring; the abstract’s evidence concerns generated molecular candidates and their evaluated properties, rather than demonstrated therapeutic effectiveness.
neurips-2025-prior-guided-flow-matching-.tldr: PAFlow guides molecule generation with protein-interaction predictions and a learned atom count, reporting improved affinity scores on CrossDocked2020.

paragraphs: This paper examines when imposing geometric structure on a neural network helps its performance. Group equivariance constrains a model’s response to transformations so that it follows a prescribed relationship. The authors study the trade-offs of these constraints through theory and point-cloud experiments, using a unified architecture called Rapidash to compare equivariant and non-equivariant variants under controlled conditions.

Their results suggest that stronger equivariance constraints can improve performance when they fit the task’s geometry. Simply increasing representation capacity does not fully close the observed gaps. The study covers segmentation, regression, and generation, emphasizing that the usefulness of a structural prior depends on what the task requires the model to distinguish.

The authors also separate two forms of geometric intervention. Explicit symmetry breaking through reference frames consistently improves performance in their study. Breaking equivariance through geometric input features can help when those features align with task geometry. These findings support task-specific model selection: architectural constraints, reference frames, and input features each affect how geometric information becomes available to the network.
neurips-2025-probing-equivariance-and-sy.tldr: Controlled point-cloud studies show that equivariance and symmetry breaking can improve performance when their geometric assumptions suit the task.

paragraphs: RAG-IGBench evaluates question-answering systems that produce interleaved text and images using retrieved information. Such answers must succeed in several ways at once: the text should be useful, the images should be appropriate, and the two should agree. Metrics focused on a single modality can miss problems in how the combined response works.

The benchmark uses publicly available social-platform content and targets systems that connect multimodal language models to external image-text retrieval. Its evaluation measures text quality, image quality, and consistency between them. The authors test both open-source and proprietary models to examine their capabilities and limitations in this combined generation setting.

The proposed metrics show high correlation with human assessments, supporting their relevance to how people judge the outputs. Models fine-tuned on the benchmark’s training data also improve across multiple benchmarks. These findings provide evidence for both the evaluation design and the usefulness of the training set. The contribution treats the relationship between words and images as a central part of answer quality.
neurips-2025-rag-igbench-innovative-eval.tldr: RAG-IGBench evaluates retrieved image-text answers using modality quality and cross-modal consistency, with metrics that correlate strongly with human judgments.

paragraphs: TDLSR addresses learning when each example can have multiple feature views and multiple labels, but some features and annotations are missing. The challenge combines heterogeneous information, relationships among labels, and incomplete observations. Missingness can therefore disrupt both the representation of an example and the connections used to predict its labels.

The framework constructs a sample topology for each view and a graph of prototype associations. These structures support proximity-aware imputation and class representatives that encode label relationships. It also uses principles of information shift, interaction, and orthogonality to separate information within the learned representations, reducing redundant content and distortion as information is combined.

Label semantics then guide the identification of discriminative features shared across views and features specific to individual views. This also refines how different views contribute to particular labels. The paper theoretically studies representation properties and generalization, and reports effective results on public datasets and real-world applications. Its central contribution is coordinating missing-data handling with label-specific representation learning, so these parts of the problem inform one another.
neurips-2025-theory-driven-label-specifi.tldr: TDLSR combines graph-based imputation and label-guided representations to learn from data with missing feature views and incomplete labels.

paragraphs: TPP-SD speeds up sampling from Transformer temporal point processes, which generate sequences of events over time. Powerful Transformer models can be costly to sample from autoregressively. The paper adapts speculative decoding from language models by identifying a structural connection between that technique and the thinning algorithms used for temporal point processes.

A smaller draft model proposes multiple candidate events, and the larger target model verifies them. This arrangement uses the cheaper model to prepare candidates while retaining the target model’s role in determining the sampling distribution. The framework preserves the same output distribution as autoregressive sampling, so its stated benefit is faster generation without changing that distribution.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report speedups of two to six times while producing samples from the same distributions as standard methods. Ablation studies examine how draft length and draft-model size affect efficiency. The findings show that speculative generation can extend beyond language tokens to event sequences, with the observed speed benefit depending on the sampling configuration examined in the experiments.
neurips-2025-tpp-sd-accelerating-transfo.tldr: TPP-SD uses draft-and-verify event sampling to preserve a Transformer point process’s output distribution while achieving reported 2–6× speedups.

paragraphs: UniMotion brings motion simulation, prediction, and planning into one framework for autonomous driving. These tasks have different objectives, but all require understanding interactions among traffic participants and how movement develops through space and time. The paper argues that separate specialized models limit shared learning, cross-task generalization, and scalability.

The framework uses a decoder-only Transformer with interaction modes and training strategies tailored to the different tasks. This lets the tasks share representations and undergo joint optimization while retaining their individual requirements. The same framework can subsequently be fine-tuned for a particular task when specialization is useful.

Experiments on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset report robust generalization and effective integration from joint training. With additional fine-tuning, UniMotion reaches state-of-the-art performance across a range of motion tasks. The distinction between these stages matters: joint training supports a reusable motion representation, while the strongest reported task results involve further specialization. The work provides empirical evidence that related motion tasks can benefit from a common architecture and coordinated training.
neurips-2025-unimotion-a-unified-motion-.tldr: UniMotion shares a Transformer across driving simulation, prediction, and planning, with joint-training benefits and state-of-the-art results after task-specific fine-tuning.
